```{r}
#| output: false
#| echo: false

library(renv)
renv::load()
library(targets)
library(here)
tar_config_set(
  store = here::here("_targets")
)
source(here::here("R", "analyse-coux.R"))
source(here::here("R", "contributions.R"))
source(here::here("R", "sem.R"))
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(bipartite)
library(glmmTMB)
library(piecewiseSEM)

guild_colors <- c(pollinator = "#2a78d6", plant = "#eb6834")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11))
```

We measure what each pollinator contributes to its community, to later ask
with a structural equation model how much of that contribution depends on
its network role (normalised degree) and its position in trait space
(originality). We measure each pollinator's contribution to:

1. the **robustness** of the network;
2. plant **functional diversity**.

## Robustness

Robustness $R$ is the area under the curve of the fraction of plants
surviving as pollinators are removed one by one, a plant going extinct once
all its pollinators are gone [@Memmott-Waser-Price-2004b]. We average it over
1000 random removal orders. $R_i^\text{first}$ is the same average when
pollinator $i$ is always removed first. The contribution of $i$ is

$$\Delta R_i = R - R_i^\text{first}$$

that is, how much less robust the network is when $i$ is lost first rather
than an average pollinator (`compute_robustness_contributions()` in
`R/contributions.R`).

```{r}
web_list <- tar_read(web_list)

robustness_contributions <- tar_read(robustness_contributions) |>
  left_join(
    tar_read(net_metrics) |>
      filter(guild == "pollinator") |>
      select(site, species, normalised_degree),
    by = join_by(site, species)
  ) |>
  group_by(site) |>
  mutate(n_pollinators = n()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(n_plants = vapply(web_list, nrow, integer(1))[site]) |>
  group_by(site) |>
  mutate(cascade_relative = (cascade - mean(cascade)) / n_plants) |>
  ungroup()

spearman <- function(x, y) sprintf("%.2f", cor(x, y, method = "spearman"))
```

```{r}
ggplot(robustness_contributions, aes(x = delta_r_first)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 0.02, fill = guild_colors[["pollinator"]], color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  labs(x = expression(Delta * R[i]), y = "Number of pollinator-site records")
```

**$\Delta R_i$ sums to zero within a site.** A random order can be drawn by
picking the first pollinator (probability $1/n$ each) and shuffling the
rest, so $R$ is the mean of the $R^\text{first}_i$:

$$R = \frac{1}{n} \sum_i R^\text{first}_i
\quad \Rightarrow \quad \sum_i \Delta R_i = 0$$

We estimate $R$ this way, so the sum is exactly zero.
$\Delta R_i$ is thus relative: how much more a pollinator matters than the
others at its site. At two-pollinator sites, the two species get opposite
values.

```{r}
robustness_contributions |>
  filter(n_pollinators == 2) |>
  select(site, species, cascade, delta_r_first) |>
  mutate(delta_r_first = round(delta_r_first, 3)) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("site", "species", "cascade", "ΔR"))
```

**$\Delta R_i$ measures how much more plant species are lost after removing $i$
removal, compared with an average pollinator removal.** Let $\text{c}_i$ be the
number of plants whose only pollinator is $i$, $\bar c$ its site average and $P$
the number of plants. When every plant has a single pollinator,

$$\Delta R_i = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\text{c}_i - \bar c}{P}.$$

```{r}
ggplot(
  robustness_contributions,
  aes(x = cascade_relative, y = delta_r_first)
) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = 0.5, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50"
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7, color = guild_colors[["pollinator"]]) +
  labs(
    x = "Relative cascade, (cascade - site mean) / plants",
    y = expression(Delta * R[i])
  )
```

$|\Delta R_i|$ is smaller at richer sites
(ρ = `r spearman(abs(robustness_contributions$delta_r_first), robustness_contributions$n_pollinators)`
with the number of pollinators). It reflects that richer networks are more
robust to extinctions.

**Link with normalised degree.** $\Delta R_i$ rises with normalised degree
(ρ = `r spearman(robustness_contributions$delta_r_first, robustness_contributions$normalised_degree)`),
as the degree → contribution path of the SEM expects.

```{r}
ggplot(
  robustness_contributions,
  aes(x = normalised_degree, y = delta_r_first)
) +
  geom_jitter(
    width = 0.01, height = 0, alpha = 0.7, color = guild_colors[["pollinator"]]
  ) +
  labs(x = "Normalised degree", y = expression(Delta * R[i]))
```

## Contribution to functional diversity

We measure plant functional diversity (FD) with a dendrogram
[@Petchey-Gaston-2002]: an average-linkage (UPGMA) tree of the 14 plant
species in trait space, the same space as for originality. The FD of a set
of plants is the total length of the branches connecting them, so a single
plant has FD = 0. We build one tree for all sites, so branch lengths are
comparable between sites.

Below, *P. marginata* is the only pollinator of *Lolium* at `daiburnam`.
Losing it costs a third of the plants but half of the FD, because *Lolium*
sits alone on a long branch.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5
plot_fd_removal(tar_read(plant_fd_tree), web_list[["daiburnam"]], "p_marginata")
```

We then repeat the robustness calculation with the fraction of the site's
plant FD retained instead of the fraction of plants alive. $\Delta FD_i$ is
defined like $\Delta R_i$, with the same removal orders
(`compute_fd_contributions()` in `R/contributions.R`). It also sums to zero
within a site.

```{r}
contributions <- robustness_contributions |>
  left_join(tar_read(fd_contributions), by = join_by(site, species))
fd_fit <- lm(delta_fd_first ~ delta_r_first, contributions)
contributions <- contributions |>
  mutate(fd_residual = resid(fd_fit))
```

A pollinator removes FD only through the plants it alone visits, so
$\Delta FD_i$ closely follows $\Delta R_i$
(R² = `r sprintf("%.2f", summary(fd_fit)$r.squared)`,
slope = `r sprintf("%.2f", coef(fd_fit)[[2]])`; dashed line 1:1 below).
The slope is above 1 because the last plant has FD = 0, so FD falls
faster than the number of plants. We use the residual of the regression,
rather than the raw difference $\Delta FD_i - \Delta R_i$, so that it does
not depend on $\Delta R_i$. It is positive when the plants $i$ supports are
functionally distinct, and negative when they have functional equivalents
at the site.

```{r}
ggplot(contributions, aes(x = delta_r_first, y = delta_fd_first)) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50"
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7, color = guild_colors[["pollinator"]]) +
  labs(x = expression(Delta * R[i]), y = expression(Delta * FD[i]))
```

**What explains the residual?** The residual sums to zero within a site, so
we correlate it with each candidate after subtracting the site mean. The
candidates are the pollinator's traits and network role, and the plants it
supports (`compute_plant_support()`). Excess FD loss is the share of the
site's FD lost with the plants $i$ alone visits, minus the share of plants
lost.

```{r}
residual_check <- contributions |>
  left_join(tar_read(plant_support), by = join_by(site, species)) |>
  left_join(
    tar_read(pollinator_trait_network) |>
      select(
        site, species, originality, originality_w, uniqueness, hs,
        abundance
      ),
    by = join_by(site, species)
  ) |>
  mutate(log_abundance = log(abundance))

candidates <- c(
  "Originality" = "originality",
  "Weighted originality" = "originality_w",
  "Uniqueness" = "uniqueness",
  "Normalised degree" = "normalised_degree",
  "HS" = "hs",
  "Abundance (log)" = "log_abundance",
  "Uniqueness of plants visited" = "partner_uniqueness",
  "Uniqueness of plants only it visits" = "sole_uniqueness",
  "Excess FD loss" = "excess_fd_loss"
)

residual_check |>
  group_by(site) |>
  mutate(across(all_of(unname(candidates)), \(x) x - mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(fd_residual, all_of(candidates)) |>
  pivot_longer(-fd_residual, names_to = "candidate") |>
  filter(!is.na(value), !is.na(fd_residual)) |>
  group_by(candidate = factor(candidate, names(candidates))) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    rho = cor(fd_residual, value, method = "spearman"),
    p = cor.test(fd_residual, value, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)$p.value
  ) |>
  mutate(across(c(rho, p), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Candidate", "n", "ρ", "p"))
```

None of the pollinator's own traits, nor its network role or abundance,
predicts the residual. The traits of the plants it supports do: the residual
is high when the plants a pollinator alone visits are functionally unique.
Only pollinators with at least one such plant have a value for that
candidate (n = 42). Excess FD loss is close to a restatement of the
residual rather than an explanation of it. Among the explanatory candidates
defined for all pollinators, the uniqueness of the plants visited is the
best.

## Structural equation model

We ask how a pollinator's position in trait space (originality) and its
network role (normalised degree) shape its contributions, with two paths:

1. originality → normalised degree → $\Delta R_i$ → $\Delta FD_i$;
2. originality → uniqueness of the plants visited → $\Delta FD_i$.

Since $\Delta R_i$ is in the $\Delta FD_i$ equation, the second path acts on
the part of $\Delta FD_i$ that $\Delta R_i$ does not explain, i.e. the
residual above. We fit a piecewise SEM [@Lefcheck-2016], with one
`glmmTMB` mixed model per response: binomial for normalised degree,
Gaussian otherwise, with random effects of site and species unless their
variance is zero (`fit_contribution_sem()` in `R/sem.R`).

```{r}
sem_summary <- summary(tar_read(contribution_sem), .progressBar = FALSE)
sem_coefs <- sem_summary$coefficients
sem_p <- function(response, predictor) {
  p <- sem_coefs$P.Value[
    sem_coefs$Response == response & sem_coefs$Predictor == predictor
  ]
  sprintf("%.2f", p)
}
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
plot_sem_paths(tar_read(contribution_sem))
```

Arrows show standardised coefficients (`plot_sem_paths()` in `R/sem.R`).
The model fits: no missing path is needed (Fisher's C =
`r sprintf("%.1f", sem_summary$Cstat$Fisher.C)`, df =
`r sem_summary$Cstat$df`, p = `r sprintf("%.2f", sem_summary$Cstat$P.Value)`).

- **Traits do not predict network role.** Originality has no clear effect
  on normalised degree (p = `r sem_p("normalised_degree", "originality_z")`).
- **Network role drives the contribution to robustness**, and through it
  most of the contribution to plant FD.
- **Traits act on plant FD through the plants visited.** Original
  pollinators visit less unique plants
  (p = `r sem_p("partner_uniqueness", "originality_z")`), and visiting
  unique plants raises $\Delta FD_i$ beyond what $\Delta R_i$ predicts.

The last link came out of an exploratory search among candidates, and it
weakens without *A. mellifera*, which sits at the extreme of most axes. We
return to its role in the discussion.
